questionText: In the CAP theorem, what does the "P" (Partition tolerance) mean?
option1: The database splits a big table into partitions, so that each node stores only a part of the data
option2: The system keeps working even when the network between its nodes breaks and messages between them are lost
option3: The system can lose any single disk or server without losing data, because every node holds a copy
option4: The system divides its users into groups and sends each group to a different data center or region
correctOptionExplanation: A partition is a communication break between nodes (a cut cable, a dead router). It has nothing to do with splitting a table into partitions or shards.

questionText: People say "you cannot just pick any 2 of the 3 in CAP". Why is Partition tolerance not really optional for a system spread over several servers?
option1: Partition tolerance is the cheapest property to build, so every system gets it automatically without any design effort
option2: The theorem only forbids combining consistency with availability, so partitions never affect the other two properties in practice
option3: Partitions only happen between data centers in different countries, so a single region can always ignore the P
option4: Networks between servers do fail, so partitions will happen; the real choice is between consistency and availability when they do
correctOptionExplanation: You cannot buy a network that never breaks. So P is a fact of life, and CAP really asks what you give up while a partition lasts: correct answers (C) or always answering (A).

questionText: Mumbai and Delhi each hold a copy of the seat data, and the network between them works fine. Which of Consistency and Availability can the system offer right now?
option1: Only one of them, because CAP forbids offering both at any moment, even while the network is healthy
option2: Neither of them, because two copies in different cities can never agree on the data quickly enough
option3: Both: with no partition, the copies sync and every request is answered with up-to-date data
option4: Only availability, because syncing between cities always takes too long to guarantee consistency
correctOptionExplanation: CAP only bites at the moment a partition happens. While the network works, you get both, as in the first animation of class 57.

questionText: Zoya books seat A7 on the Mumbai copy. A moment later Aman asks the Delhi copy about A7. In a strongly consistent system, what must Delhi do?
option1: Show whatever it currently has, even if A7 is still free, and fix the difference later when time permits
option2: Show A7 as free to Aman, because the booking belongs to the Mumbai copy and Delhi serves only its own users
option3: Wait a fixed ten seconds and then answer with its own copy, no matter what Mumbai has told it so far
option4: Show A7 as booked, or refuse to answer if it cannot confirm with Mumbai; it must never show A7 as free
correctOptionExplanation: Consistency means every read sees the latest write, or gets an error. A stale "free" answer is exactly what a consistent system refuses to give.

questionText: In CAP, what does "Availability" promise?
option1: Every request to a working node gets an answer (not an error), even though the answer may be out of date
option2: The system never goes down for any reason, so the servers are guaranteed to be running 24 hours a day
option3: Every request is answered with the latest data, and requests that cannot be answered correctly are retried
option4: The system answers fast, within a few milliseconds, even when many users send requests at the same time
correctOptionExplanation: In CAP, available means: a node that is up always responds. It says nothing about speed, and it allows stale data, which is the whole trade-off.

questionText: The network between Mumbai and Delhi breaks. Aman asks the Delhi copy to book A7. What does a CP system do?
option1: It books A7 anyway, because refusing a customer is worse than a rare double booking in a CP system
option2: It books A7 on Delhi and silently copies the booking to Mumbai through a second, hidden network path
option3: It redirects Aman to the Mumbai copy through the broken link, which is how CP systems keep users happy
option4: It returns an error or waits, because it cannot confirm with Mumbai and refuses to risk selling the seat twice
correctOptionExplanation: CP chooses to be correct and gives up availability for that request: Aman sees an error, but nobody gets wrong data and the seat is never sold twice.

questionText: Same broken network, but now an AP system. Zoya booked A7 on Mumbai, and Aman books A7 on Delhi. What is the situation when the network is repaired?
option1: Both bookings were accepted, so the copies disagree: seat A7 was sold twice and someone gets a refund
option2: Delhi rejects the second booking automatically, because AP systems always remember what the other copies did
option3: Nothing happened, because both copies held the same data all along and the broken network only delayed messages
option4: The system rolls both bookings back, so neither Zoya nor Aman gets the seat and the show starts with an empty seat
correctOptionExplanation: AP answers every request from whatever data the node has. During the partition, Delhi thought A7 was free, so two people were promised the same seat.

questionText: A movie ticketing app stores seat bookings in two data centers. When the link between them breaks, what should it favour, and why?
option1: Availability (AP): every user should always get a happy answer, and double bookings can be sorted out later at no cost
option2: Availability (AP): seats are just numbers in a table, so a short disagreement between the copies never matters
option3: Consistency (CP): a double-booked seat is worse than showing an error for a few minutes
option4: Neither: a ticketing app must keep both properties, since the theorem allows it when both data centers are in one country
correctOptionExplanation: Wrong data costs real money and angry customers here, so seats pick C. This is the rule of thumb: when wrong data is worse than an error, choose CP.

questionText: Two bank servers lose contact. A customer with Rs 100 sends Rs 100 from each server at the same moment. Which choice protects the bank?
option1: Availability (AP): both transfers go through, and the bank collects the missing Rs 100 later from the customer
option2: Consistency (CP): refuse one of the transfers rather than let the balance be spent twice on two servers
option3: Availability (AP): each server approves its own transfer, which is how all banking systems are designed to work
option4: Neither: the bank is not affected, because balances are numbers and numbers cannot become inconsistent
correctOptionExplanation: Money must never be spent twice, so a bank prefers an error ("try again later") over two servers disagreeing about the balance.

questionText: A video platform stores like counts in two data centers. When the link between them breaks, each side keeps accepting likes. Is that a sensible choice?
option1: Yes, AP fits: the counts may be a little behind for a while, and nobody is harmed by that
option2: No, likes must be CP: a count that differs for a few minutes between two cities is a serious data error
option3: No, because AP means the likes are lost for ever once the network is repaired and the copies are merged
option4: Yes, but only if the platform refuses every like during the partition, since that is what AP actually means
correctOptionExplanation: A like count a few seconds behind harms nobody, so availability wins. After the partition heals, the copies catch up (eventual consistency).

questionText: An online store lets users add items to their cart even while a partition separates two data centers, and merges the two versions of the cart afterwards. What does this choose?
option1: Consistency (CP): the cart waits until both data centers agree, so a user may see an error while adding an item
option2: Neither: merging carts later means the store has found a way around the CAP theorem completely
option3: Availability (AP): adding to the cart must always work, and the versions are merged afterwards
option4: Partition tolerance is dropped: the store simply assumes that the network between its data centers will not break
correctOptionExplanation: A lost "add to cart" is a lost sale, and a merged cart is cheap to fix, so carts are a classic AP choice.

questionText: During sign-up, two users on two sides of a partition both pick the username "zoya". Which choice keeps usernames unique?
option1: Availability (AP): both users get the name, and the system sorts out the duplicate when the network returns
option2: Availability (AP): usernames are not important data, so a duplicate for a few minutes is completely harmless
option3: Neither choice is needed, because usernames are just strings and two strings can never conflict with each other
option4: Consistency (CP): one side must refuse or wait, because both cannot be told the name is free
correctOptionExplanation: Uniqueness cannot be checked when the copies cannot talk to each other. Keeping a name unique means saying "not now" on one side, which is the CP choice.

questionText: A coordination service stores "which server is the current leader". During a partition, two nodes each say "I am the leader". Why is that a problem, and what should the service prefer?
option1: Two leaders can both act on the same data and corrupt it, so it should prefer consistency (CP)
option2: Two leaders double the capacity, so it should prefer availability (AP) and keep both of them running
option3: Two leaders are harmless because they vote again once the network heals, so AP is the safe default here
option4: It is not a problem, because only the nodes in the biggest data center are counted as leaders anyway
correctOptionExplanation: Two leaders at once (split brain) is dangerous. Tools like ZooKeeper and etcd choose CP: the side without a majority stops acting as a leader.

questionText: A messaging app shows "last seen 2 minutes ago". During a partition, some users see an older "last seen" time. Is that acceptable?
option1: Yes, an AP choice: a slightly stale last-seen time harms nobody, and the value catches up later
option2: No, last seen is financial-grade data and must be exactly the same on every server at all times
option3: No, because a stale value means the system lost its availability and must return an error instead
option4: No, because an AP system must become consistent within one second after a partition or the data is lost
correctOptionExplanation: Nobody is hurt by a slightly old last-seen time, so keeping the app responsive (A) beats exactness (C). Feeds, views and status indicators are all AP.

questionText: After a partition heals, Mumbai shows 102 likes and Delhi shows 101, while the real total is 103. What do the copies do next in an AP like counter?
option1: They keep their own numbers for ever, because each copy owns the likes that came from its own city
option2: They each take the higher of the two numbers, so both settle on 102 and one like is lost
option3: They exchange the likes they missed and both end at 103: this is eventual consistency
option4: They freeze until an administrator picks the correct total by hand and restarts both copies
correctOptionExplanation: AP systems accept disagreement for a while and then reconcile. Each copy sends the other the likes it missed, so both converge to 103.

questionText: What does "eventual consistency" promise?
option1: All copies show the same value at every instant, but a write may be delayed before it is accepted by the system
option2: If no new writes arrive, all copies will eventually show the same value, but it does not say how soon
option3: All copies reach the same value within exactly one second, because the sync always completes in time
option4: Copies may disagree for ever, as it only promises that each copy is valid when looked at on its own
correctOptionExplanation: It is a promise about the end state, not about timing. For a while users may see different values; given quiet time, the copies agree.

questionText: Zoya posts a comment on the Mumbai copy, then refreshes, and her request goes to the lagging Delhi copy. Her comment is missing. What is a common fix?
option1: Make every comment wait until all copies in the world have it, so the write itself becomes much slower for every user
option2: Show her an error and ask her to post the comment again, since the first post is lost for good
option3: Delete the Delhi copy, because only one copy of the comments is allowed in an AP system
option4: Read your own writes: send her reads to the copy she wrote to, or wait until the other copy has caught up
correctOptionExplanation: The system stays AP, but the user at least sees her own changes. This is the "read your own writes" fix from the class 57 animation.

questionText: An app uses a single database server with no copies at all. Does the CAP trade-off apply to it?
option1: Yes, the single server must still give up one of consistency or availability at every single moment
option2: Not in the same way: CAP is about copies separated by a network, and one node has no partition between copies
option3: Yes, because every server is secretly built from several nodes that each choose between AP and CP
option4: No, because a single server is always both fully consistent and fully available, even when it crashes
correctOptionExplanation: CAP describes the choice you face when data is replicated and the links between copies can fail. With one node, a crash simply makes it unavailable.

questionText: A MongoDB replica set splits into a group of 2 members and a group of 1 member, and the old primary is in the group of 1. What happens by default?
option1: Both groups keep accepting writes on their own primary, and the data is merged later, so no write is ever refused
option2: The group of 2 elects a new primary and keeps taking writes; the lone member cannot accept writes (CP-leaning)
option3: All three members stop completely, because a replica set cannot work while the network is partitioned
option4: The lone old primary keeps accepting writes, because a primary never gives up its role until it crashes
correctOptionExplanation: Only the side with a majority can elect a primary (class 58 failover). The minority side gives up availability to avoid two diverging copies, so MongoDB leans CP by default.

questionText: Cassandra lets each query choose how many replicas must answer. What changes when you ask for QUORUM instead of ONE?
option1: Reads are less consistent but faster, because fewer replicas take part and no node has to wait for the others
option2: Nothing changes for consistency, because Cassandra always writes every change to all nodes at once
option3: Reads are more consistent, but queries can fail when replicas are unreachable: availability is traded for consistency
option4: Queries become more available as well as more consistent, because quorum removes the need for replicas
correctOptionExplanation: Waiting for a majority of replicas gives fresher answers but needs more nodes to be reachable. Some databases let you pick the CAP trade-off per query.

questionText: A system stops accepting writes on one side of a partition, so its two copies can never diverge. Which property did it give up on that side?
option1: Availability: requests on that side get errors, but the data stays consistent
option2: Consistency: the two copies now disagree, because one side stopped hearing from the other side
option3: Partition tolerance: the system broke down completely as soon as the network failed between the two sides
option4: Nothing: stopping writes protects all three properties at once, so CAP is not violated in any way
correctOptionExplanation: Refusing requests is a loss of availability. The system survived the partition (P) and stayed correct (C), so A is what it paid.

questionText: Select ALL the true statements about the CAP theorem.
option1: During a network partition, a system must choose between consistency and availability
option2: When there is no partition, a system can offer both consistency and availability
option3: A CP system may return errors to some requests during a partition
option4: An AP system never returns stale data, because it always asks every copy first
option5: CAP says that a distributed database can never be fast
correctOptionExplanation: The choice only appears during a partition, CP answers with errors when it cannot be sure, and AP may return stale data. CAP says nothing about speed.

questionText: Select ALL the data that is a good fit for AP (availability first).
option1: Like and view counts on a video
option2: A social media news feed
option3: Product reviews and comments
option4: The balance in a bank account
option5: Which seat a customer has booked for a show
correctOptionExplanation: Slightly stale counts, feeds and comments hurt nobody and catch up later. Balances and seat bookings must not be wrong, so they lean CP.

questionText: Select ALL the data that is a good fit for CP (consistency first).
option1: Seat bookings for a movie show
option2: Bank balances and money transfers
option3: A check that a username is not already taken
option4: The number of likes on a photo
option5: A "trending now" list on the home page
correctOptionExplanation: Booking a seat, moving money and keeping names unique all break if two copies disagree. Like counts and trending lists tolerate being a little behind.

questionText: A movie app has both seat bookings and trailer like counts. How should it treat the two when the network between its data centers breaks?
option1: Pick one choice for the whole app, because mixing CP and AP data in one system is not allowed
option2: Make everything CP, since consistency is always better and users never mind seeing errors
option3: Choose per kind of data: seat bookings and payments lean CP, while like counts and feeds lean AP
option4: Make everything AP, since availability is always better and wrong data can be fixed by customer support
correctOptionExplanation: CAP is a per-data decision, not a per-company one. Real systems use CP stores for money and seats and AP stores for likes and feeds, just as the animation shows.

questionText: Which sentence sums up the CAP theorem best?
option1: Any distributed database must pick two of Consistency, Availability and Partition tolerance and drop the third for good
option2: Networks will break (P); when they do, each piece of data must choose between being correct (C) and always answering (A)
option3: Consistency and availability are the same property seen from two angles, so a system can always have both, even during a partition
option4: A system can have all three if it uses enough servers and a fast enough network between its data centers
correctOptionExplanation: The popular "pick 2 of 3" slogan hides the real point: partitions are not optional, so the choice is C versus A at the moment of a partition.
